Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- As Hayden Henshaw was being rushed to the doctor's office after becoming ill, his father heard that his son's classmates had been struck with the deadly swine flu virus like the one sweeping through Mexico. Swine flu commonly affects pigs and occasionally infects people in contact with pigs. Patrick Henshaw called his wife immediately to have Hayden checked for it. Later, they received the bad news. Hayden had become the third confirmed case of swine flu at his Texas high school. It is a virus that has killed 68 people in Mexico and infected at least eight people in the United States. Health officials arrived at the Henshaws' house Friday and drew blood from the whole family, then told them to stay inside and away from the public, Henshaw told CNN. The whole family is quarantined indefinitely, according to CNN-affiliate KABB. Henshaw said his family was shocked when they got the news about their son. "Stunned. My wife was having a panic attack," Henshaw told the affiliate. U.S. health officials have expressed concern about U.S. cases of a swine flu virus that has similar characteristics to the fatal virus in Mexico. More than 1,000 people have fallen ill in Mexico City in a short period of time, U.S. health experts said. "This situation has been developing quickly," Richard Besser, acting director of the Atlanta, Georgia-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), said Friday. "This is something we are worried about." Besser said all of the eight U.S. patients have recovered.  Watch for more on the U.S. cases » . New York health officials said Friday they were testing about 75 students at a school in New York City for swine flu after the students exhibited flu-like symptoms this week. A team of state health department doctors and staff went to the St. Francis Preparatory School in the borough of Queens on Thursday after the students reported cough, fever, sore throat, aches and pains. Test results are expected as early as Saturday. The new virus has genes from North American swine influenza, avian influenza, human influenza and a form of swine influenza normally found in Asia and Europe, said Nancy Cox, chief of the CDC's Influenza Division. Swine flu is caused by a virus similar to a type of flu virus that infects people every year but is a strain typically found only in pigs -- or in people who have direct contact with pigs. There have, however, been cases of person-to-person transmission of swine flu, the CDC said. CNN's David Alsup contributed to this report.

The teenager, whose identity has not been released to protect his privacy, began experiencing flu-like symptoms earlier this week before being tested and confirmed as positive for the H1N1 virus, according to local health department officials. He is reported to be recovering at home.

"When we identify a confirmed case, our priority is to limit contact with others," the health official explained. "That includes close family members who may have been exposed."

The Texas case adds to a growing number of confirmed infections across several states, including California, Kansas, and New York. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has been closely monitoring the situation and has urged Americans to take basic precautions.

"We are seeing this virus in multiple locations, and we expect that number to rise," a CDC official said during a press briefing. "This is a rapidly evolving situation."

## What Is Swine Flu?

The H1N1 virus is a respiratory illness that shares genetic characteristics with strains found in pigs, though health officials emphasize that it cannot be contracted by eating properly cooked pork. Symptoms are similar to seasonal flu and include fever, cough, sore throat, body aches, and fatigue.

The World Health Organization has been in close contact with health authorities in both the United States and Mexico and has warned that the virus has the potential to become a broader public health concern.

# New Swine Flu Strain Spreads Concern as Cases Climb in North America

When 9-year-old Marcus Delgado came home from school last Tuesday complaining of chills and a headache, his mother Elena assumed it was an ordinary cold. By Thursday, his fever had spiked to 103 degrees, and a persistent cough left him exhausted and struggling to eat.

"I've raised three kids, so I know what a regular flu looks like," said Elena Delgado, 41, from her family's home in suburban San Diego. "But something about this felt different. He couldn't shake it."

A visit to their pediatrician led to a nasal swab and, three days later, a phone call that would upend the family's week: Marcus had tested positive for the new strain of H1N1 swine influenza that health authorities have been monitoring with growing alarm.

## A Widening Outbreak

The Delgado family's experience is being repeated in households across the region as public health officials track an outbreak that has jumped international borders and prompted emergency responses on both sides.

The World Health Organization has convened emergency meetings to assess the threat, while the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has stepped up surveillance efforts nationwide.

"We are dealing with a novel virus, and that means there are significant unknowns," said a CDC spokesperson during a press briefing this week. "Our primary concern is the potential for sustained human-to-human transmission, which appears to be occurring."

## By the Numbers

The epicenter of the outbreak remains Mexico, where authorities have reported more than 1,600 suspected cases and dozens of deaths potentially linked to the virus. Officials in Mexico City have closed schools, canceled public events, and urged residents to avoid crowded spaces.

In the United States, confirmed cases have been reported across several states, including California, Texas, Kansas, and New York. While the U.S. count remains lower and no deaths have yet been recorded domestically, health officials caution that these figures are likely an undercount, given the lag in testing and reporting.

"The numbers we see today represent where the outbreak was days ago, not where it is right now," one epidemiologist noted.

## Understanding the Virus

Scientists studying the pathogen say it is a novel H1N1 strain—a genetic mix containing elements of swine, avian, and human influenza viruses. This reassortment is what makes the virus particularly noteworthy: because it differs substantially from seasonal flu strains, most people have little or no existing immunity.

Despite its name, health officials emphasize that swine flu is not contracted by eating pork products. The virus spreads much like seasonal influenza—through respiratory droplets when infected people cough or sneeze, and by touching contaminated surfaces.

Symptoms mirror those of ordinary flu: fever, cough, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, and in some cases vomiting and diarrhea. Antiviral medications such as oseltamivir have shown effectiveness against the strain when administered early.

## What Comes Next

For the Delgado family, treatment came quickly, and Marcus is now recovering at home under quarantine. "The doctor caught it in time," Elena said. "But I keep thinking about the families who might not know what they're dealing with."

Health authorities are urging the public to take preventive measures: frequent handwashing, covering coughs, staying home when sick, and seeking medical care for severe symptoms. Officials have stopped short of recommending drastic measures like travel bans but say they are prepared to escalate their response as the situation develops.

"This is a moment for vigilance, not panic," the CDC spokesperson said. "But we are watching this very, very closely."

---

# Health Officials Race to Contain New Swine Flu Strain as Cases Mount

*Novel H1N1 virus prompts federal response; parents anxious as schools weigh closures*

By CNN Staff

Federal health authorities scrambled this week to respond to a growing outbreak of a novel swine flu virus that has sickened dozens across several states, prompting a public health emergency declaration and urgent calls for calm as investigators work to understand the scope of the threat.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention confirmed multiple cases of the new H1N1 influenza strain, a virus that has caught the attention of scientists because of its unusual genetic composition and its apparent ability to spread from person to person.

"We are responding aggressively," said Dr. Richard Besser, the CDC's acting director, during a briefing with reporters. "We want to be out in front of this. As we look for cases, we are likely to find more, and we are likely to find them in more places."

Besser emphasized that the situation remains fluid and urged Americans to take practical precautions rather than panic.

"This is a time when we need to be prepared, but not alarmed," he said. "Covering your cough, washing your hands frequently, staying home when you are sick — these are simple steps that make a real difference."

## An Unusual Genetic Mix

What has scientists particularly interested is the makeup of the virus itself. According to CDC researchers, this H1N1 strain is a genetic combination unlike anything seen circulating before in humans.

Laboratory analysis shows the virus contains genetic material from multiple sources — including gene segments from swine influenza viruses found in North American and Eurasian pig populations, as well as segments with avian and human influenza origins. This reassortment, in which flu viruses swap genetic components, produced a new strain to which most people have little or no existing immunity.

Because the virus is novel, health officials say there is no vaccine currently available that specifically targets it, though laboratory testing indicates the strain is susceptible to two antiviral medications, oseltamivir and zanamivir, sold under the brand names Tamiflu and Relenza.

## A Parent's Worry

For families caught in the early wave of infections, the outbreak has brought anxiety and disruption.

Maria Alvarez, whose teenage son fell ill after his school reported a cluster of cases, described the uncertainty of the past several days.

"When they told us it might be this new flu, my heart just dropped," Alvarez said. "You hear 'swine flu' and you don't know what to think. My son had a high fever, body aches, he was exhausted. As a mother, you feel helpless."

She said her son is now recovering, but the experience left her shaken.

"They told us to keep him home, keep him away from his little sister, watch for anything getting worse," she said. "You just want someone to tell you your kids are going to be okay."

## What Comes Next

Officials said they are monitoring the outbreak closely and coordinating with state and local health departments, as well as international partners. Some schools with confirmed cases have temporarily closed as a precaution while investigations continue.

Besser cautioned that the coming days would be critical in determining the virus's behavior.

"Influenza is unpredictable," he said. "We are learning more every hour, and we will continue to share what we know with the American people as quickly as we can."

Health officials are advising anyone experiencing flu-like symptoms — including fever, cough, sore throat, body aches and fatigue — to contact their health care provider and to stay home to avoid infecting others.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

**Health officials scramble to contain outbreak as suspected infections emerge in Texas, New York**

Federal health authorities confirmed a growing number of swine flu cases across the southern United States on Friday, as an outbreak that has sickened hundreds in Mexico appears to have crossed the border, prompting quarantines and heightened surveillance at schools and hospitals nationwide.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said laboratory testing had verified multiple human infections of a novel H1N1 influenza strain, a virus containing genetic material from swine, avian, and human flu viruses. Officials expressed concern that the strain appears capable of sustained human-to-human transmission.

## Texas Family Quarantined

In Guadalupe County, Texas, a family of four has been placed under voluntary home quarantine after two members tested positive for the virus. Health workers in protective equipment visited the household this week to collect samples and deliver antiviral medication.

"We were told to stay home, keep our distance from each other where possible, and monitor our temperatures," said the family's father, who asked that his name be withheld. "It started with what felt like a normal cold. Now we're watching the news and realizing this is something bigger."

Local health officials emphasized that all four family members were in stable condition and responding to treatment with antiviral drugs such as oseltamivir.

## Suspected Cases at New York Prep School

In New York City, administrators at a Queens preparatory school closed their doors after several students fell ill with flu-like symptoms following spring break, some reportedly returning from trips to Mexico.

Dozens of students reported fevers, sore throats, and body aches. City health officials collected specimens and sent them to federal laboratories for confirmation.

"Out of an abundance of caution, we have suspended classes and are cooperating fully with health authorities," a school spokesperson said. Parents lined up outside the campus seeking information as anxiety spread through the community.

## CDC Urges Calm, Vigilance

At a press briefing in Atlanta, CDC officials sought to balance urgency with reassurance.

"We are taking this very seriously, and we are responding aggressively," a CDC spokesperson said. "But we also want the public to understand that seasonal influenza causes illness every year. The steps people can take are familiar ones: wash your hands frequently, cover your coughs, and stay home if you are sick."

Experts noted that the current cases have ranged from mild to moderate in the United States, in contrast to the more severe outcomes reported in Mexico—a discrepancy officials said they were still working to understand.

"We don't yet have a complete picture," the spokesperson added. "The genetic makeup of this virus is unusual, and we are working around the clock with state, local, and international partners to track its spread and develop appropriate countermeasures, including a potential vaccine."

## What Comes Next

The CDC has recommended that clinicians report suspected cases promptly and consider antiviral treatment for confirmed infections. Officials also advised travelers to and from affected regions of Mexico to monitor their health closely.

The World Health Organization convened emergency consultations to assess whether the outbreak could constitute a public health emergency of international concern.

For now, health authorities are asking Americans to remain informed but not panicked.

"Preparedness, not fear, is what protects communities," the CDC official said. "We've planned for situations like this, and we're putting those plans into action."
